title: Habla --- Telling Somebody To Do Something

lessons.title: habla — telling somebody to do something
lessons.gloss: telling somebody to do something — and the form is one you have had since your seventh chapter

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Say "he speaks." (Habla.) Hold that word. You are about to be told it does a second job you have never been shown.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: you already have it

segments.text: To tell somebody you address as tú to do something, use the he/she form of the present.
Habla. — Speak. Come. — Eat. Vive. — Live.
That is the whole rule, and it costs you nothing. Habla was already in your mouth as "he speaks"; the same two syllables, said to somebody, are an order.

utterances: verb: hablar. he/she does: habla. you, do it: habla.
verb: comer. he/she does: come. you, do it: come.
verb: vivir. he/she does: vive. you, do it: vive.

segments.text: The column repeats. That is not an oversight in the table.

Spanish does this often enough that it is worth naming as a habit: rather than inventing a new form for every job, it reuses one and lets context sort it out. Habla said about somebody is a statement; habla said to somebody is a command, and nobody has ever confused the two.
The name for this form is the imperative, from Latin imperāre, "to command."

That imper- is a word you already know in English clothes. An emperor is literally one who commands; an empire is the thing he commands. The grammar term and the political ones are the same root, which is a fair description of what the form does: it is the sentence shape that expects to be obeyed.

segments.instruction: "habla" as a statement, then "¡Habla!" as an order — same word, different job

segments.prompt: Tell somebody you call tu to eat.

feedback.incorrect: Come — the he/she form, said to somebody.

segments.prompt: Which form do you use to give a tu command?

feedback.incorrect: The he/she form of the present.

segments.prompt: Which two English words share a root with imperative?

feedback.correct: One who commands, and the thing commanded.
feedback.incorrect: Emperor and empire — both from imperare, to command.

segments.text: Tell somebody to speak. (Habla.) Which form is that? (The he/she present — nothing new.) What does imperāre mean? (To command — as in emperor.) Next: eight verbs that refused, and every one of them is a single syllable.
